issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of witnessed other trauma or with the rest of the profile. 'People cycling' and 'my ex' imply very different personal meanings, and neither has an evident connection to the reported threat items (general unsafety, sleep vigilance, hypervigilance). With only a weak Triggers → Threat link active, the triggers should still plausibly cue the threat state; these two triggers appear idiosyncratic in unrelated directions and are hard to reconcile as part of the same trauma-linked pattern.

This relationship-specific reminder suggests a different interpersonal trauma context that is not represented elsewhere in Threat or other nodes, making the trigger set clinically incoherent for the same index trauma.

vignette: Ahmed is a 29-year-old Middle Eastern man who works as a train conductor. He has been single for several years and recently came to therapy after experiencing intense psychological distress following a traumatic event at his workplace. On one particularly hectic day, while operating the train, Ahmed witnessed another passenger being severely injured by a sudden malfunction in the railway system. The vivid images of blood and visible injuries have left him shaken. Since that fateful incident, Ahmed has become increasingly sensitive to specific triggers that are intimately tied to the traumatic event. One such trigger is tactile sensations related to temperature changes on his skin, which remind him of the cold sweat he felt when witnessing the passenger's injury. The visual presence of blood and visible injuries also brings back a flood of distressing memories. These triggers have become so potent that they often lead Ahmed into a heightened state of threat perception. Ahmed had come to believe that even when others tell him he is safe, it remains impossible for him to trust their reassurances. This has led to an ongoing sense of hypervigilance and an almost obsessive need to stay alert at all times. He finds it difficult to fall asleep because his mind is constantly on guard, replaying the traumatic scene and imagining potential threats lurking around every corner. The specific tactile trigger of temperature changes further exacerbates Ahmed's threat perception. Whenever he feels a sudden change in skin temperature, whether from cold air conditioning or warm sunlight, he becomes immediately alert and tense. This physical sensation serves as an unwelcome reminder of the traumatic event, propelling him into a state of heightened arousal and fear. His hypervigilance has also extended to his daily work environment. As a train conductor, Ahmed is constantly aware of potential hazards around him, making it challenging for him to focus on routine tasks. The sight of even minor injuries or blood in the station or on passengers can trigger intense anxiety and panic attacks. This has led to several close calls where he nearly missed critical safety checks due to his heightened state of alertness. Ahmed's fear of not being able to trust his own sense of safety is deeply intertwined with these triggers. The more often he encounters tactile sensations, visual cues related to blood or injuries, the more he struggles to believe that any situation is truly safe. This has created a self-reinforcing cycle where each encounter with a trigger strengthens his perception of threat and further erodes his ability to relax. Despite the severity of these symptoms, Ahmed had managed to maintain his job for several weeks after the incident by avoiding certain routes or shifts where he would be exposed to potential triggers. However, as time went on, this avoidance became increasingly difficult to sustain. His colleagues noticed a decline in his performance and offered him support, but their reassurances only added to his distress. What finally brought Ahmed to seek help was a particularly stressful day at work when he nearly caused an accident due to his hypervigilance. He realized that his current state of mind was not only affecting his job but also putting the safety of others at risk. His most significant fear is losing control and causing harm again, while what he hopes for most is finding a way to regain trust in his own ability to stay safe and secure. Through therapy, Ahmed aims to address these triggers and rebuild his sense of trust and safety, ultimately hoping to return to a normal life where the traumatic event no longer dictates his daily experiences.
